title: Momentum, Gravitation and Rotation
bigQuestion: What quantities stay the same when objects collide, spin and orbit, and how do those conservation rules let us predict what happens next?

story.title: Bringing Apollo 13 Home
story.kicker: In April 1970 an explosion crippled a spacecraft 200,000 miles from Earth. The crew came home on the same physics that had sent them out.
paragraphs: On the evening of April 13, 1970, about 56 hours after launch, astronaut Jack Swigert flipped a switch to stir the oxygen tanks in the Apollo 13 service module. A damaged wire inside one tank sparked. The tank burst, tore open the side of the module, and dumped the oxygen the fuel cells needed to make electricity and water. Within minutes the command module was dying. Swigert radioed Houston that they had a problem.

The ship was already committed. It had left Earth's orbit two days earlier and was falling toward the Moon under gravity alone. The three astronauts could not simply turn around. In space there is no road to turn on; a spacecraft goes where its velocity and gravity carry it, and changing that path costs fuel and a working engine. The command module's big engine sat next to the explosion, and nobody trusted it.

So the crew moved into the lunar module, Aquarius, a small craft built to land two people on the Moon for two days, not to keep three people alive for four. Its descent engine became the ship's only reliable way to change velocity. Mission Control planned burns that used the Moon itself. The ship would swing around the far side and let lunar gravity bend its path back toward Earth, a route called a free-return trajectory.

Every burn was a problem in momentum and gravitation. Fire the engine for too long or in the wrong direction, and the ship would miss the narrow corridor where Earth's atmosphere could catch it without either bouncing it back into space or burning it up. The crew aligned the ship by sighting the Sun and Earth through a small telescope, and fired the descent engine for a few minutes after rounding the Moon to speed the trip home.

There were other problems, including carbon dioxide building up in a cabin whose filters were the wrong shape, solved with cardboard, tape and a sock. But the path home was pure physics: the conservation of momentum, the law of gravitation and the orbital mechanics worked out by Kepler and Newton centuries earlier. On April 17 the command module splashed down in the Pacific Ocean, and all three astronauts walked off the recovery ship.
story.think: Apollo 13 could not turn around the way a car can. What is different about changing direction in space, and why did the Moon's gravity turn out to be a help rather than a threat?

lessons.title: Momentum and Impulse
lessons.mainIdea: Momentum is mass times velocity, and a force acting over a time interval changes momentum by an amount called impulse.
reading: A bowling ball rolling slowly and a tennis ball flying fast can be equally hard to stop. What they share is *momentum*, the product of mass and velocity, written p = mv. Momentum is a vector that points the way the velocity points. Its unit is the kilogram meter per second. A 0.15 kg baseball at 40 m/s carries 6 kg·m/s; a 1,500 kg car at 30 m/s carries 45,000 kg·m/s.

Newton actually wrote his second law in terms of momentum: the net force on an object equals the rate at which its momentum changes. Multiply both sides by the time the force acts and you get *impulse*. Impulse equals force times time, and it equals the change in momentum. A big force for a short time and a small force for a long time can produce the same change in momentum. That single sentence is the physics of every catch, crash and cushion.

A baseball catcher pulls his glove back as the ball arrives. The ball's momentum change is fixed by its speed and mass, but by letting the stop take longer, the catcher lowers the force on his hand. A boxer rolls with a punch for the same reason. The seat belt from the last chapter is an impulse device: same momentum change, longer time, smaller force. The area under a force-time graph is the impulse, just as the area under a velocity-time graph is displacement.

Impulse also runs the other way. A rocket engine delivers force over a long burn, and the momentum the ship gains is the whole area under that force-time curve. The Apollo 13 crew needed a precise change in momentum to reach Earth. They got it by burning a known engine for a timed number of seconds, and the stopwatch mattered as much as the engine.

words.d: mass times velocity, a vector measured in kg·m/s
force times the time it acts, equal to the change in an object's momentum
a graph whose area under the curve equals the impulse delivered
how fast a quantity changes per unit of time

look.title: Catching the Same Ball Two Ways
look.text: A student catches a 0.5 kg ball moving at 10 m/s. First she holds her hands stiff and the ball stops in 0.02 s. Then she lets her hands ride back with the ball, and it stops in 0.2 s. In both cases the ball ends at rest, so its momentum changes by the same 5 kg·m/s.
look.prompt: Calculate the average force in each case. Which catch stings, and what did the moving hands actually change?

check.q: What is the momentum of a 1,200 kg car moving at 25 m/s?
choices: 48 kg·m/s
300 kg·m/s
check.why: Momentum is mass times velocity: 1,200 times 25 equals 30,000 kg·m/s.

check.q: A 20 N force acts on a cart for 3 s. By how much does the cart's momentum change?
choices: 6.7 kg·m/s
23 kg·m/s
60 kg·m/s
It depends on the cart's mass
check.why: Impulse equals force times time, 20 times 3, or 60 N·s, and impulse equals the change in momentum regardless of the mass.

check.q: Why does an air bag reduce injury in a crash?
choices: It reduces the change in the passenger's momentum
It adds an outward force that cancels the crash
It reduces the passenger's mass
It increases the time over which the momentum changes, lowering the force
check.why: The momentum change is fixed by the speed. Spreading it over a longer time makes the average force smaller.

lessons.title: Conservation of Momentum
lessons.mainIdea: When no outside force acts on a system, its total momentum stays the same, no matter how its parts push on one another.
reading: Two skaters stand still on smooth ice, facing each other. One pushes the other. Both move apart, and the lighter skater moves faster. Before the push the total momentum was zero. After it, one skater's momentum points left and the other's points right, and the two add to zero again. The push was an internal force, a third-law pair inside the system, and internal forces cannot change the total momentum.

That is the law of *conservation of momentum*. For any *system* of objects, if the net external force is zero, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. The reason is Newton's third law. Every force one part exerts on another is matched by an equal and opposite force back. Each pair delivers equal and opposite impulses, so the changes in momentum cancel within the system.

The law makes hard problems easy. A 2 kg cart at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg cart at rest and the two stick together. Total momentum before: 6 kg·m/s. After, the combined 3 kg mass must carry the same 6 kg·m/s, so it moves at 2 m/s. You never needed to know the force between the carts or how long it acted. Momentum bookkeeping skips the messy middle of the collision entirely.

*Recoil* is the same law seen from the other side. A rifle kicks backward when the bullet goes forward. A rocket moves forward because it throws exhaust backward at high speed, which is why rockets work in empty space with nothing to push against. Every burn of Aquarius's descent engine was a momentum trade: hot gas one way, spacecraft the other, and the sum unchanged.

words.d: the rule that the total momentum of a system does not change when no net external force acts on it
the set of objects chosen for analysis, so that forces between them count as internal
the backward motion of an object that launches something forward, so that total momentum stays the same
a force from outside the chosen system, the only kind that can change the system's total momentum

look.title: Newton on Forces in Pairs
look.text: In explaining his third law, Newton wrote that if you press a stone with your finger, the finger is also pressed by the stone, and that if a horse draws a stone tied to a rope, the horse is drawn back toward the stone by the same amount, so that the stone's progress forward and the horse's progress forward are hindered by equal forces.
look.cite: Isaac Newton, Principia, 1687, paraphrased from Motte's translation
look.prompt: Use Newton's horse and stone to explain why the total momentum of horse plus stone cannot be changed by the rope between them.

check.q: A 60 kg skater at rest pushes a 40 kg skater, who moves off at 3 m/s. What is the 60 kg skater's velocity?
choices: 2 m/s in the opposite direction
3 m/s in the opposite direction
4.5 m/s in the opposite direction
Zero, because she did the pushing
check.why: Total momentum stays zero. The 40 kg skater has 120 kg·m/s one way, so the 60 kg skater needs 120 kg·m/s the other way, which is 2 m/s.

check.q: Why can a rocket accelerate in empty space?
choices: It pushes against the thin gas of space
It throws exhaust backward, and conservation of momentum sends the rocket forward
Gravity from the planet pulls it along
Its engine creates momentum from fuel energy
check.why: The exhaust's backward momentum is balanced by the rocket's forward momentum. No outside surface is needed.

check.q: A 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s hits a 3 kg cart at rest and they stick together. What is their speed afterward?
choices: 4 m/s
1 m/s
2 m/s
8 m/s
check.why: Momentum before is 12 kg·m/s. The combined 6 kg mass must carry 12 kg·m/s, so it moves at 2 m/s.

lessons.title: Collisions in Two Dimensions
lessons.mainIdea: Momentum is conserved separately along each axis, and whether kinetic energy is also conserved decides if a collision is elastic or inelastic.
reading: On a pool table the cue ball strikes a stationary ball at an angle. The two balls leave in different directions, and neither one goes the way the cue ball was going. Yet if you add their momentum vectors, head to tail, the sum points exactly along the cue ball's original path with the same length. Momentum is conserved as a vector, so it is conserved along the x axis and the y axis separately.

That makes two-dimensional collisions a matter of bookkeeping in two columns. Write the total x-momentum before and after; they must match. Do the same for y. If a 2 kg puck moving east at 3 m/s hits a puck at rest and afterward moves northeast, the pucks' combined northward momentum must be zero, so the second puck has to move somewhat southward. Crash investigators use exactly this reasoning, working backward from skid marks to the speeds before impact.

Collisions come in kinds. In an *elastic collision* the total kinetic energy after equals the total before. Billiard balls and colliding steel bearings come close. In an *inelastic collision* some kinetic energy turns into heat, sound and deformation. Momentum is still conserved. If the objects stick together it is *perfectly inelastic*, and the loss of kinetic energy is the largest possible. Car crashes are inelastic, and the crumpling that eats the energy is by design.

Momentum and energy are different conserved quantities, and mixing them up is the most common error. Two identical clay balls moving toward each other at equal speeds stick and stop. Momentum: zero before, zero after, conserved. Kinetic energy: plenty before, none after, all turned to heat. Nothing was violated. Kinetic energy is only one form of energy, while momentum has no other form to hide in.

words.d: a collision in which total kinetic energy is the same before and after
a collision in which some kinetic energy becomes heat, sound or deformation; momentum is still conserved
a collision in which the objects stick together and move as one afterward
the energy of motion, equal to one half of mass times speed squared

look.title: The Intersection Crash
look.text: A 1,000 kg car heading north at 20 m/s collides at an intersection with a 2,000 kg truck heading east at 10 m/s. The vehicles lock together. The wreck slides off along a single straight line, and the skid marks let a police investigator measure its direction.
look.prompt: Find the northward and eastward momentum before the crash. In what direction, roughly, should the skid marks point, and what is the wreck's speed just after impact?

check.q: Which quantity is conserved in every collision, elastic or inelastic, when no outside force acts?
choices: Kinetic energy
Speed of each object
Total momentum
Velocity of each object
check.why: Momentum conservation depends only on the absence of external forces. Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.

check.q: A moving puck strikes a stationary puck and afterward both move off at angles on the same side of the original line. Can this happen?
choices: Yes, if they both slow down
No, because momentum perpendicular to the original line must stay zero
Yes, if the collision is elastic
No, because both pucks must stop
check.why: Before the collision there was no sideways momentum. If both pucks went to the same side, their sideways momenta would add instead of cancel.

check.q: Two identical clay balls moving toward each other at equal speeds collide and stop. What happened to their kinetic energy?
choices: It was destroyed, which violates conservation
It went into the momentum of the combined ball
It was stored as potential energy
It became heat, sound and deformation
check.why: Energy is conserved, but kinetic energy can change into other forms. In a perfectly inelastic collision it does so as much as possible.

lessons.title: Center of Mass
lessons.mainIdea: Every object or system has a center of mass that moves as if all the mass were there and all external forces acted on it, even while the parts tumble.
reading: Toss a hammer end over end across a room. The head and handle trace wild loops, but one point on the hammer follows a smooth parabola, exactly like a thrown ball. That point is the *center of mass*, the average position of all the mass in the object. For a uniform ruler it sits at the middle. For a hammer it sits near the heavy head. For a doughnut it sits in the hole, where there is no material at all.

The center of mass obeys a simple rule. Its motion depends only on the external forces on the system and the total mass, as if everything were concentrated there. That is why a fireworks shell that bursts in midair still has a center of mass moving along the original arc, even as fragments fly everywhere. It is also why conservation of momentum can be stated another way: with no external force, the center of mass moves at constant velocity.

Balance depends on the center of mass too. An object resting on a surface tips over when its center of mass moves past the edge of its base of support. Wide stances and low centers of mass are stable; that is why a wrestler crouches and why a tall bus takes corners slowly. A high jumper using the flop technique arches so that her center of mass passes below the bar while her body, piece by piece, passes over it.

You can find the center of mass of a flat shape by hanging it from two different points and drawing a vertical line down from each. The lines cross at the center of mass. In space, a two-body system like the Earth and Moon orbits around their shared center of mass, which lies inside the Earth but well away from its center. Astronomers find unseen planets by watching stars wobble around a center of mass they share with something dark.

words.d: the average position of the mass in an object or system; the point that moves as if all the mass were there
the area on the ground between the points where an object touches it
tending to return to position after a small tip, because the center of mass stays over the base
the small back-and-forth motion of a star or planet around a shared center of mass

look.title: The Exploding Shell
look.text: A fireworks shell is launched at an angle and, at the top of its arc, bursts into two unequal pieces. The lighter piece flies straight backward, toward the launch point. Ignore air resistance. A camera on a tripod records the burst and the fall of both pieces.
look.prompt: Where must the heavier piece go? Describe how the center of mass of the two pieces moves after the burst, and explain why.

check.q: Where is the center of mass of a uniform ring, like a hula hoop?
choices: At the center of the ring, where there is no material
On the ring itself, at the top
On the ring itself, at the bottom
It has no center of mass
check.why: The center of mass is the average position of the mass. For a symmetric ring that average is the empty center.

check.q: A wrench is thrown and spins as it flies. Which point on the wrench follows a smooth parabola?
choices: The heavy end
The light end
The center of mass
No point does, because it spins
check.why: Only gravity acts externally, so the center of mass moves like a simple projectile while the rest of the wrench rotates around it.

check.q: A tall bookshelf tips over when leaned forward. What has happened at the instant it starts to fall?
choices: Its mass has shifted to the top shelf
Friction with the floor has vanished
Its weight has increased
Its center of mass has passed beyond the edge of its base
check.why: An object stays upright as long as the vertical line through its center of mass falls within its base of support.

lessons.title: Torque and Balance
lessons.mainIdea: Torque is the turning effect of a force, equal to force times lever arm, and an object in rotational equilibrium has zero net torque as well as zero net force.
reading: Try to open a door by pushing near the hinge. It barely moves. Push at the handle with the same force and it swings easily. The difference is not the force but where it acts. *Torque* is the turning effect of a force, and it equals the force times the *lever arm*, the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force. Torque is measured in newton meters. Long wrenches, long handles and long oars all exist to multiply torque.

A force pointed straight at the pivot has no lever arm and no torque, however large it is. Only the part of the force perpendicular to the lever counts. That is why you pull a wrench at a right angle to its handle and why a bicycle pedal delivers the most torque when the crank is horizontal. Torque, like force, is a vector; by convention a counterclockwise turn is positive and clockwise is negative.

For an object to be in *rotational equilibrium*, the torques must add to zero, just as forces must for ordinary equilibrium. A seesaw balances when the weight on one side times its distance from the pivot equals the weight on the other side times its distance. A 30 kg child 2 m from the center balances a 60 kg adult sitting 1 m from the center. Cranes, bridges and bookshelf brackets are designed with the same two rules: net force zero, net torque zero.

Your body works by torque. Muscles attach close to joints, so they must pull with large forces to hold modest loads at the hand. Holding a 5 kg bag with the forearm level means the biceps pulls with something like 150 N, because its lever arm is short and the bag's is long. The reward is that a small muscle contraction moves the hand a long way, fast. Nature traded force for speed.

words.d: the turning effect of a force, equal to the force times its lever arm, in newton meters
the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line along which a force acts
the point or axis about which an object rotates
the condition in which all torques on an object add to zero, so its rotation does not change

look.title: Balancing the Plank
look.text: A 4 m uniform plank of mass 10 kg rests on a pivot at its center. A 20 kg child sits at the far right end, 2 m from the pivot. A second student wants to balance the plank by placing a 40 kg sandbag somewhere on the left side.
look.prompt: Where should the sandbag go? Explain why the plank's own weight can be ignored here, and what would change if the pivot were not at the plank's center.

check.q: A 10 N force is applied at the end of a 0.5 m wrench, perpendicular to the handle. What torque does it produce?
choices: 20 N·m
5 N·m
check.why: Torque equals force times lever arm: 10 times 0.5 equals 5 N·m.

check.q: Why is it hard to open a door by pushing close to the hinges?
choices: The door is heavier near the hinges
Friction is greater near the hinges
The lever arm is short, so the torque is small
The force points away from the pivot
check.why: Torque depends on the distance from the pivot. Near the hinge that distance, the lever arm, is small.

check.q: A 40 kg child sits 1.5 m from a seesaw's pivot. Where must a 30 kg child sit to balance it?
choices: 1.5 m from the pivot
1.125 m from the pivot
3 m from the pivot
2 m from the pivot
check.why: Torques must be equal: 40 times 1.5 equals 60. The 30 kg child needs 60 divided by 30, or 2 m.

lessons.title: Angular Momentum
lessons.mainIdea: Spinning objects carry angular momentum, which stays constant when no outside torque acts, so pulling mass inward makes a spin faster.
reading: A figure skater spins with arms out, then pulls them in and spins dramatically faster. No one pushed her. She simply rearranged her own mass. Rotation has its own version of momentum, called *angular momentum*, and it is conserved when no external torque acts. Angular momentum depends on how fast something spins and on how its mass is spread out around the axis, a quantity called *moment of inertia*.

Moment of inertia plays the role that mass plays in straight-line motion. Mass far from the axis counts much more than mass near it. Pulling the arms in reduces the skater's moment of inertia, so to keep angular momentum constant her spin rate must go up. Divers tuck to somersault faster and stretch out to slow their rotation before entering the water. Gymnasts, cats and falling astronauts all do the same.

Angular momentum is also a vector, pointing along the spin axis, and its direction is conserved as well as its size. That is why a spinning top stays up and a moving bicycle stays balanced far more easily than a stopped one. A gyroscope in a spacecraft holds its axis fixed in space, giving Apollo's guidance system a reference direction while the ship itself turned. A spinning turntable on the lab bench resists being tilted for the same reason.

On the largest scales angular momentum shapes the universe. A slowly turning cloud of gas collapses under gravity into a star, and as its mass draws inward it spins faster, flattening into a disk. Planets form in that disk, all circling the same way, which is why the planets of the solar system orbit in nearly the same plane and the same direction. Collapsed stars called pulsars, no larger than a city, can spin hundreds of times per second for the same reason.

words.d: the rotational version of momentum, depending on spin rate and how mass is spread around the axis
a measure of how hard an object is to spin up, larger when mass is farther from the axis
a spinning wheel whose axis resists being turned, used to hold a reference direction
the line around which an object rotates

look.title: The Turntable and the Weights
look.text: A student sits on a freely rotating stool holding a heavy weight in each hand, arms stretched out, and a friend spins her slowly. She pulls the weights in to her chest and speeds up. She pushes them out again and slows down. Then she tries the same trick while holding nothing at all, and the change is much smaller.
look.prompt: Explain each observation using angular momentum and moment of inertia. Why did the empty-handed version barely work?

check.q: A spinning skater pulls her arms in. What happens to her angular momentum and her spin rate?
choices: Both increase
Angular momentum stays the same and spin rate increases
Angular momentum increases and spin rate stays the same
Both stay the same
check.why: No external torque acts, so angular momentum is conserved. Her moment of inertia drops, so her spin rate must rise.

check.q: Which change increases an object's moment of inertia about its axis?
choices: Spinning it faster
Moving its mass closer to the axis
Moving its mass farther from the axis
Making it slide instead of roll
check.why: Moment of inertia grows when mass is placed farther from the axis of rotation; spin rate does not change it.

check.q: Why do all the planets orbit the Sun in nearly the same plane and direction?
choices: The Sun's gravity pulls them into line over time
Collisions between planets aligned their orbits
Earth's orbit set the pattern for the others
They formed from one spinning cloud whose angular momentum flattened it into a disk
check.why: As the cloud collapsed it spun faster and settled into a disk, and the planets inherited that shared rotation.

lessons.title: Universal Gravitation
lessons.mainIdea: Every mass attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
reading: The apple falls; the Moon does not fall away. Newton's insight was that both are the same event. The Moon is falling toward Earth all the time, but it also moves sideways fast enough that the ground curves away beneath it. Gravity that reaches the top of a tree, he reasoned, should reach the Moon too, though weaker with distance. He worked out how much weaker: the pull drops with the *square of the distance*.

The law of *universal gravitation* says the force between any two masses equals G times the first mass times the second, divided by the distance between their centers squared. G is the *gravitational constant*, about 6.67 times 10 to the minus 11 newton meters squared per kilogram squared. That tiny number is why you do not feel the pull of a nearby building. It takes a planet-sized mass to make the force noticeable.

The law explains why g is 9.8 m/s² on Earth's surface and 1.6 m/s² on the Moon. Plug in Earth's mass and radius and out comes 9.8. The acceleration does not depend on the falling object's mass, because that mass cancels, which is why a hammer and a feather fall together on the airless Moon, as an Apollo 15 astronaut demonstrated on camera in 1971. Double your distance from Earth's center and the pull drops to one quarter.

Newton could not measure G. In 1798 Henry Cavendish did, with a delicate torsion balance: two small lead balls on a rod suspended by a fine wire, drawn toward two large lead balls. The twist of the wire measured a force smaller than a grain of sand's weight. With G known, the mass of the Earth followed, and then the mass of the Sun. One measurement in a quiet shed weighed the solar system.

words.d: Newton's law that every pair of masses attracts with a force proportional to their product and inversely to distance squared
G, about 6.67 times 10 to the minus 11 N·m²/kg², which sets the strength of gravity
a relationship in which a quantity falls to one quarter when the distance doubles
an instrument that measures a tiny force by the twist it gives a fine wire

look.title: Newton's Own Account of the Moon
look.text: Newton later recalled that the idea of gravitation came to him while sitting in a garden, when the fall of an apple set him thinking about why the power of gravity should not extend as far as the Moon, and whether the same force might hold the Moon in its orbit.
look.cite: Reported by William Stukeley from a conversation with Newton in 1726, paraphrased
look.prompt: Newton's question was not 'why does the apple fall' but 'how far up does the pull reach.' Why is the second question the more powerful one?

check.q: If the distance between two masses is tripled, the gravitational force between them becomes
choices: one third as large
one ninth as large
three times as large
nine times as large
check.why: Gravity follows an inverse square law. Three squared is nine, so the force drops to one ninth.

check.q: Why do a hammer and a feather fall together on the Moon?
choices: The Moon's gravity is too weak to tell them apart
The feather is heavier on the Moon
With no air, the acceleration due to gravity is the same for every mass
The Moon pulls harder on lighter objects
check.why: The falling object's mass cancels out of the acceleration. On Earth only air resistance makes the feather slower.

check.q: What did Cavendish's 1798 experiment make possible?
choices: The first measurement of the speed of light
The discovery that the Moon orbits Earth
Proof that gravity does not reach beyond the atmosphere
A measured value of G, and from it the mass of the Earth
check.why: Measuring the tiny force between lead balls gave G, and with G known Earth's mass could be calculated from g and Earth's radius.

lessons.title: Kepler's Laws
lessons.mainIdea: Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one focus, sweep out equal areas in equal times, and have periods whose squares scale with the cubes of their orbital sizes.
reading: Before anyone knew why planets move, Johannes Kepler worked out how. He inherited decades of careful naked-eye measurements of Mars from the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe. For years Kepler tried to fit those positions to circles, and the best circle missed by about eight minutes of arc, a small angle but far larger than Tycho's errors. Kepler trusted the data over the circle and threw the circle out.

His *first law* says each planet moves on an *ellipse*, a stretched circle with two special points called foci, and the Sun sits at one focus. Most planetary orbits are nearly circular; Earth's distance from the Sun varies by only about 3 percent over a year. Mars is more stretched, which is why its orbit gave the circle away. Comets follow extremely stretched ellipses and spend most of their time far from the Sun.

The *second law* says a line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun the planet moves fast; far away it crawls. This is conservation of angular momentum in disguise. The *third law*, found ten years later, says the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the Sun. A planet four times farther out takes eight times longer to go around.

Newton showed that all three laws follow from an inverse square force. That was the decisive test of universal gravitation: a single law derived by thinking about falling apples reproduced patterns Kepler had dug out of Tycho's tables. The third law now works in reverse. Measure how far and how fast a moon orbits a planet, and you can weigh the planet without ever visiting it.

words.d: a stretched circle with two focus points; the sum of the distances from any point on it to the two foci is constant
one of the two special points inside an ellipse; the Sun sits at one focus of each planet's orbit
the time an orbiting body takes to complete one trip around
Kepler's rule that the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the average orbital distance

look.title: Planetary Periods Around the Sun
look.cite: NASA planetary fact sheet, rounded; 1 AU is the average Earth-Sun distance
look.prompt: For each planet, compare the square of the period with the cube of the distance in AU. How close do they come to being equal, and what does that say about Kepler's third law?

check.q: Where is the Sun located in a planet's elliptical orbit?
choices: At one focus of the ellipse
At the exact center of the ellipse
At both foci at once
Outside the ellipse
check.why: Kepler's first law places the Sun at one of the two foci, not at the center. The other focus is empty.

check.q: A comet on a highly stretched orbit is nearest the Sun. Compared with its speed when farthest away, it moves
choices: at the same speed
much faster
much slower
in the opposite direction
check.why: Equal areas in equal times means the comet sweeps a short, fat slice near the Sun quickly and a long, thin slice far away slowly.

check.q: An asteroid orbits at 4 AU from the Sun. About how long is its year?
choices: 4 Earth years
16 Earth years
8 Earth years
64 Earth years
check.why: Period squared equals distance cubed in these units. Four cubed is 64, and the square root of 64 is 8 years.

lessons.title: Orbits and Satellites
lessons.mainIdea: A satellite stays in orbit because its sideways speed is just enough that, as it falls toward Earth, the surface curves away beneath it.
reading: Newton imagined a cannon on a high mountain. Fire the ball slowly and it lands nearby. Fire it faster and it lands farther away. Fire it fast enough and the ground curves away as quickly as the ball falls, so it never lands at all. It circles the Earth and comes back to the cannon. That thought experiment, drawn in a book published after his death, is the whole idea of a *satellite*. Orbiting is falling with enough sideways speed to keep missing.

The speed needed depends only on the mass of the planet and the distance from its center. For a circular orbit, gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force, and the equation gives the *orbital velocity* as the square root of G times the planet's mass divided by the orbital radius. Closer orbits are faster. Just above Earth's atmosphere a satellite must move at nearly 8 km/s and completes a lap in about 90 minutes. The Moon, 60 times farther out, moves at about 1 km/s and takes a month.

Different jobs need different orbits. Weather and spy satellites fly low for sharp pictures. Navigation satellites sit at medium altitudes. A satellite placed about 35,800 km above the equator takes exactly one day to go around, so it hangs over the same spot on the ground. That is a *geostationary* orbit, and it is where communication and many weather satellites live, so that a fixed dish can point at them.

To leave a planet entirely you need *escape velocity*, the speed at which an object's kinetic energy matches the energy needed to climb out of the planet's gravity well. For Earth it is about 11.2 km/s from the surface. Apollo 13's problem was that its ship had that kind of speed and needed to give some of it back precisely, so that Earth's gravity could capture it into a path that ended in the atmosphere at the right angle.

words.d: any object that orbits a planet or star, natural like the Moon or artificial like a weather satellite
the speed needed for a circular orbit at a given distance, faster for closer orbits
an orbit about 35,800 km above the equator whose period matches Earth's rotation, so the satellite stays over one spot
the minimum speed needed to leave a planet's gravity entirely, about 11.2 km/s from Earth's surface

look.title: Escape Velocity From the Surface
look.prompt: The Moon's escape velocity is about a fifth of Earth's. Why did the small ascent stage of a lunar module have enough fuel to leave the Moon, when leaving Earth took a rocket the size of a skyscraper?

check.q: What keeps a satellite in orbit around Earth?
choices: Its engines fire continuously to hold it up
It is beyond the reach of gravity
It falls toward Earth while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing
An outward force balances gravity
check.why: Gravity is the only force, pulling it into a curve. Its sideways speed makes that curve match the Earth's, so it never lands.

check.q: Compared with a satellite in low orbit, a satellite in a much higher orbit moves
choices: faster, because it has farther to go
at the same speed
faster, because gravity is weaker there
slower, and takes longer to complete an orbit
check.why: Orbital velocity falls with distance, and the path is longer as well, so the period grows sharply with altitude.

check.q: Why are communication satellites often placed in geostationary orbit?
choices: They stay over one spot on Earth, so ground antennas can point at them permanently
It is the lowest orbit, giving the strongest signal
It is outside Earth's gravity
They can see the whole Earth at once from there
check.why: A one-day period matches Earth's rotation, so the satellite appears fixed in the sky above the equator.

lessons.title: Weightless on the Space Station
lessons.mainIdea: Astronauts on the International Space Station float not because gravity is absent but because they and the station are falling around Earth together.
reading: The *International Space Station* orbits about 400 km up, moving at roughly 7.7 km/s and circling the Earth about every 90 minutes. Its crew sees around 16 sunrises a day. Inside, tools drift, water forms wobbling spheres and astronauts sleep strapped to the wall. It is tempting to say there is no gravity up there. There is plenty. At 400 km Earth's pull is still about 90 percent as strong as on the ground.

The astronauts float because everything on the station, people, air, tools and the walls, is in *free fall* together. Recall the elevator with the snapped cable from the last chapter: the floor no longer pushes up, so you feel weightless even though gravity is pulling as hard as ever. The station is that elevator, falling continuously, but with enough sideways speed that it never reaches the ground. Weightlessness is the feeling of nothing pushing back.

That state, sometimes called *microgravity*, is why the station is a laboratory. Flames burn as round blue spheres because hot air does not rise. Crystals grow without settling. Bones and muscles, no longer loaded, weaken by measurable amounts each month, so astronauts exercise about two hours a day and are studied carefully on return. Their bodies are experiments in what a lifetime of standing up against gravity really does.

The station is also a lesson in the small forces this unit has ignored. Thin air at 400 km drags on it, and it loses a little altitude every day, so visiting spacecraft periodically boost it back up. The Moon's gravity and the Sun's tug on it as well. Even the ISS is not quite the ideal orbit of the equations, and keeping it there is a matter of momentum bookkeeping, done month after month.

words.d: the crewed laboratory orbiting about 400 km above Earth since the late 1990s
motion in which gravity is the only force acting, so everything falls together and feels weightless
the condition aboard an orbiting spacecraft in which objects appear weightless because they are in free fall
the slow loss of altitude a low satellite suffers because of drag from the thin upper atmosphere

look.title: The Call From Apollo 13
look.text: Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.
look.cite: Astronaut Jack Swigert, Apollo 13 air-to-ground transcript, NASA, April 13, 1970
look.prompt: The crew reported a problem calmly, in a few words. What did Mission Control need to know first, and why does a spacecraft's situation depend so much on its position and velocity at the moment of trouble?

check.q: Why do astronauts on the ISS float?
choices: There is no gravity at 400 km altitude
The station's speed cancels gravity
The station and everything in it are in free fall together
Air pressure inside the station holds them up
check.why: Gravity at the station is about 90 percent of surface gravity. Everything falls together, so nothing pushes back and they feel weightless.

check.q: In which situation would a person feel weightless on Earth?
choices: Standing in an elevator moving upward at constant speed
Standing on a scale at the equator
Sitting in a car going around a curve
Riding in an elevator whose cable has snapped, during the fall
check.why: In free fall the floor no longer pushes up, so the person experiences the same weightlessness as an orbiting astronaut.

check.q: Why must the ISS be boosted to a higher altitude from time to time?
choices: Its orbit grows larger on its own and must be corrected
Drag from the thin upper atmosphere slowly lowers its orbit
The Moon pulls it away from Earth
Its rotation slows down
check.why: Even at 400 km there is a trace of air. The drag removes a little momentum every day, and the orbit decays until a spacecraft pushes it back up.

review.q: A 0.2 kg ball moving at 10 m/s is caught and stopped in 0.05 s. What is the average force on the ball?
choices: 2 N
review.why: The momentum change is 2 kg·m/s. Impulse equals force times time, so force is 2 divided by 0.05, or 40 N.

review.q: A cannon on frictionless wheels fires a shell forward. What happens to the cannon?
choices: It stays still because it is heavier
It moves forward with the shell
It recoils backward so that total momentum stays zero
It rises off the ground
review.why: Before firing, momentum is zero. The shell's forward momentum must be matched by the cannon's backward momentum.

review.q: Which statement about a perfectly inelastic collision is correct?
choices: Kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not
Momentum is conserved and the objects stick together
Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
review.why: Momentum is conserved in every collision without external forces. In a perfectly inelastic one the objects stick, and the most kinetic energy is lost.

review.q: A meter stick balances on a pivot at its 50 cm mark. A 100 g mass is hung at the 20 cm mark. Where should a 200 g mass hang to balance it?
choices: The 65 cm mark
The 80 cm mark
The 35 cm mark
The 90 cm mark
review.why: The 100 g mass is 30 cm from the pivot, giving 100 times 30. The 200 g mass needs 15 cm on the other side, at the 65 cm mark.

review.q: A diver leaves the board spinning slowly in a stretched position, then tucks tightly. Her rotation rate
choices: stays the same because angular momentum is conserved
decreases because her moment of inertia decreases
increases because her angular momentum increases
increases because her moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum stays the same
review.why: With no external torque, angular momentum is fixed. Tucking lowers the moment of inertia, so the spin rate goes up.

review.q: The gravitational force between two objects is 100 N. If one mass is doubled and the distance between them is doubled, the force becomes
review.why: Doubling a mass doubles the force. Doubling the distance divides it by four. Together: 100 times 2 divided by 4 equals 50 N.

review.q: According to Kepler's second law, a planet moves fastest when it is
choices: farthest from the Sun
at either end of its orbit's long axis
closest to the Sun
crossing the ecliptic
review.why: The Sun-planet line sweeps equal areas in equal times, so the planet must move fastest where the line is shortest, near the Sun.

review.q: A satellite in a circular orbit fires a small rocket that increases its speed. Immediately afterward, what is true?
choices: It rises and moves into an orbit that reaches farther from Earth
It falls straight toward Earth
It continues in the same circle at higher speed
It escapes Earth's gravity at once
review.why: More speed than a circular orbit needs at that radius makes the path an ellipse that climbs to a greater distance on the far side.
